## Research overview

### Bacterial synthesis and biomedical applications of metal nanoparticles

Environmental bacteria, *Acinetobacter* species, can be induced to reduce metal
salts into nanoparticles of controlled size and shape. My doctoral and subsequent
work established the optimized conditions for silver nanoparticle synthesis,
identified lignin peroxidase as agents of the reduction, and characterised the
silver, gold and selenium particles that result. The appeal is that the synthesis
runs in aqueous environment at room temperature, without the reducing agents that
conventional routes depend on.

Biogenic nanoparticles turn out to be active where conventional antimicrobials are
struggling. We have shown silver nanoparticles disrupting *Acinetobacter* biofilms,
acting in synergy with existing antibiotics against nosocomial strains, inhibiting
*Candida albicans*, and suppressing *Mycobacterium* species. Selenium nanoparticles
from *Acinetobacter* sp. SW30 proved cytotoxic to breast cancer cells.

### Applied environmental remediation

A complementary strand applies biogenic nanomaterials and low-cost biosorbents to
pollution control. Bacteriogenic gold nanocatalysts decolorise textile dye effluent,
while banana and carrot peel waste serve as effective biosorbents for Procion
Magenta and Black Azabache dyes. A 2026 review extends this work to review the role
of engineered nano-adsorbents to close the gap of critical microplastic–nanoplastic
capture.

### Survey-based research on science education and public understanding

A separate strand of my work uses survey-based research as a vehicle to train
postgraduate students in data collection, statistical analysis and scientific
reasoning, giving them hands-on exposure to how empirical research is actually done.
Working with PG students and my colleagues, I have guided surveys across multiple
themes: educators' learning from online professional courses, public awareness and
risk perception of food-contact materials, etc. Each of these studies has been
published, turning the training exercise itself into a peer-reviewed contribution.
